titleStmt.title: Operant conditioning of spinal reflexes: from basic science to clinical therapy
titleStmt.author: Aiko K. Thompson
Jonathan R. Wolpaw

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Operant conditioning of spinal reflexes: from basic science to clinical therapy

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: As it has turned out, operant conditioning of spinal cord reflexes is both a valuable laboratory model and a potentially powerful therapeutic method.

span.label: operant conditioning of spinal reflexes
span.quote: Here we review the 35-year evolution of one promising new approach, operant conditioning of spinal reflexes.

span.label: review
span.quote: This review tracks the evolution of another basic science exploration of spinal cord plasticity into a promising new clinical therapy.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The reward contingency induces plasticity in the brain, which in turn guides and sustains the spinal cord plasticity that directly produces the reflex change — a top-down hierarchy rather than a single site of change
span.quote: Taken together, these studies showed that H-reflex conditioning depends on a hierarchy of plasticity (i.e., Figure 2C), in which the reward contingency produces plasticity in the brain that guides and maintains the plasticity in the spinal cord that is directly responsible for the H-reflex change

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Acquiring a new spinal behaviour disturbs the equilibrium serving existing behaviours, which triggers widespread adaptive change until a new equilibrium serving the enlarged repertoire is reached — and that renegotiation can repair a behaviour that trauma had impaired
span.quote: When the acquisition of a new behavior (e.g., a larger or smaller H-reflex) changes the spinal cord and disturbs older behaviors, it triggers widespread adaptive changes that arrive at a new equilibrium that serves the expanded repertoire.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A change in motoneuron sodium channels underlies both the firing-threshold shift and the slowed axonal conduction seen after down-conditioning
span.quote: A change in motoneuron sodium channels was the likely origin of the threshold shift and the reduced conduction velocity

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Compensatory adjustments in other muscles absorb the conditioned reflex change, which is why conditioning does not degrade already-normal locomotion
span.quote: It appeared that compensatory changes in the behavior of other muscles prevented soleus Hreflex conditioning from disturbing normal locomotion

span.label: The preparation was changed twice for tractability, altering what could be studied each time.
span.quote: However, the prolonged course of conditioning and the difficulties of primate research constrained mechanistic studies. These constraints drove development of the next version

span.label: The null on locomotor features is attributed to active compensation, not to absence of influence.
span.quote: However, conditioning did not disturb important locomotor features, such as right/left symmetry and step-length (Chen et al., 2005). It appeared that compensatory changes in the behavior of other muscles prevented soleus

span.label: An animal reward threshold is declared equivalent to a human verbal instruction.
span.quote: the reward criterion (i.e., equivalent to the instruction) remained constant over days and weeks

span.label: change in muscle spindle sensitivity as the mechanism of the reflex change
span.quote: initial results led to the second version of the model, operant conditioning of the monkey triceps surae H-reflex (Wolpaw, 1987), which had two advantages. It eliminated change in muscle spindle sensitivity as the mechanism of the reflex change; and it enabled conditioning in freely moving monkeys

span.label: H-reflex
span.quote: initial results led to the second version of the model, operant conditioning of the monkey triceps surae H-reflex (Wolpaw, 1987), which had two advantages. It eliminated change in muscle spindle sensitivity as the mechanism of the reflex change; and it enabled conditioning in freely moving monkeys

span.label: muscle spindle sensitivity
span.quote: initial results led to the second version of the model, operant conditioning of the monkey triceps surae H-reflex (Wolpaw, 1987), which had two advantages. It eliminated change in muscle spindle sensitivity as the mechanism of the reflex change; and it enabled conditioning in freely moving monkeys

span.label: reward criterion
span.quote: the reward criterion (i.e., equivalent to the instruction) remained constant over days and weeks

span.label: locomotor features
span.quote: However, conditioning did not disturb important locomotor features, such as right/left symmetry and step-length (Chen et al., 2005). It appeared that compensatory changes in the behavior of other muscles prevented soleus

span.label: negotiated equilibrium
span.quote: These widespread benefits are explicable in terms of the “negotiated equilibrium” hypothesis of spinal cord function (Wolpaw, 2010). According to this hypothesis, the brain maintains spinal neurons and synapses in an equilibrium that serves all the behaviors in the current repertoire

span.label: conditioning
span.quote: However, conditioning did not disturb important locomotor features, such as right/left symmetry and step-length (Chen et al., 2005). It appeared that compensatory changes in the behavior of other muscles prevented soleus

span.label: the model - THREE PREPARATIONS UNDER ONE NAME: the second version eliminated muscle spindle sensitivity as a rival mechanism and allowed freely moving animals, and the third was adopted because primate work constrained mechanistic study, so 'operant conditioning of spinal reflexes' names a succession of preparations chosen partly for tractability
span.quote: However, the prolonged course of conditioning and the difficulties of primate research constrained mechanistic studies. These constraints drove development of the next version

span.label: the locomotor null - AN ABSENCE OF NET DISTURBANCE, NOT OF INFLUENCE: conditioning did not disturb right/left symmetry or step-length, and the authors attribute that to compensatory changes in other muscles, so the unchanged measure is the output of an active adjustment rather than a system that was not affected
span.quote: However, conditioning did not disturb important locomotor features, such as right/left symmetry and step-length (Chen et al., 2005). It appeared that compensatory changes in the behavior of other muscles prevented soleus

span.label: the reward criterion - THE ANIMAL'S EQUIVALENT OF THE HUMAN INSTRUCTION: declared so in a parenthesis, which is how a rat's EMG threshold and a person's verbal task instruction come to occupy one slot in a protocol description
span.quote: the reward criterion (i.e., equivalent to the instruction) remained constant over days and weeks

span.label: builds-on → Di Giorgio (1929, 1942)
span.quote: The first effort to demonstrate such conditioning was based on Anna Di Giorgio’s demonstration that abnormal descending activity caused by a supraspinal lesion could produce change in the spinal cord that persisted after the activity ended (Di Giorgio, 1929, 1942), and on evidence of task-dependent changes in spinal reflexes (reviewed in Wolpaw et al., 1983b).

span.label: contradicts → Marshall Hall's concept of the spinal cord as a hard-wired reflex center (Hall, 1833)
span.quote: The concept of the spinal cord as a hard-wired reflex center, enunciated by Marshall Hall in the 19th century (Hall, 1833) and widely accepted through the 20th century, continues to exert strong influence, despite the extensive evidence for activitydependent spinal cord plasticity in health and disease (Mendell, 1984; Wolpaw and Carp, 1993; Wolpaw and Tennissen, 2001; Edgerton et al., 2004; Frigon and Rossignol, 2006; Zehr, 2006; Petruska et al., 2007; Courtine et al., 2009; Dietz et al., 2009; Wolpaw, 2010; Rossignol et al., 2011; Grau, 2013).

span.label: conditioning —causes→ locomotor features
span.quote: However, conditioning did not disturb important locomotor features, such as right/left symmetry and step-length (Chen et al., 2005). It appeared that compensatory changes in the behavior of other muscles prevented soleus

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: The graphs show average (± SEM) daily H-reflex sizes for 59 successful HRup rats (red upward triangles) and 81 successful HRdown rats (blue downward triangles).

span.label: Across all five model versions — monkey SSR, monkey and rat and mouse H-reflex, and human H-reflex — conditioning worked in 75-80% of subjects and left the reflex near its starting size in the rest.
span.quote: For all versions, conditioning succeeded in 75–80% of the subjects; in the other 20–25%, the reflex remained close to its initial size.

span.label: In rats and monkeys the reflex settled at roughly 175% of baseline for up-conditioning and 55% for down-conditioning.
span.quote: final reflex size was about 175% of its initial value for up-conditioning and 55% for down-conditioning

span.label: Humans reached 140% (up) and 69% (down) of baseline despite completing only 3-5% as many trials as the animals.
span.quote: In humans, who performed only 3–5% as many trials as the animals, final reflex size averaged 140% for up-conditioning and 69% for downconditioning.

span.label: The conditioning-induced reflex asymmetry outlasted removal of all descending input, proving the change resides in the spinal cord itself.
span.quote: These studies began with the demonstration that H-reflex conditioning changed the spinal cord: the reflex asymmetry produced by conditioning persisted for at least several days after all supraspinal input was removed

span.label: Down-conditioning raises the motoneuron firing threshold and slows axonal conduction velocity.
span.quote: Intracellular studies in primates and rats revealed that successful down-conditioning affected motoneuron firing threshold and reduced axonal conduction velocity

span.label: The threshold shift together with a small reduction in the Ia afferent EPSP accounts for most of the smaller reflex.
span.quote: The positive shift in threshold, plus a small decrease in the primary afferent excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP), largely explained the smaller H-reflex

span.label: Successful down-conditioning markedly increases the number of GABAergic terminals on the motoneuron.
span.quote: Particularly prominent was a marked increase in the number of identifiable GABAergic terminals with successful down-conditioning

span.label: Lesion work shows the corticospinal tract and sensorimotor cortex are necessary for reflex conditioning while other descending and ascending tracts are not.
span.quote: requires the corticospinal tract and sensorimotor cortex, but does not require other major descending or ascending spinal cord pathways

span.label: The cerebellum is required to keep the cortical plasticity alive beyond about 40 days.
span.quote: the cerebellum is essential for the long-term maintenance (beyond 40 days) of this cortical plasticity

span.label: In normal rats the conditioned reflex change leaves right/left symmetry and step length intact.
span.quote: However, conditioning did not disturb important locomotor features, such as right/left symmetry and step-length

span.label: Up-conditioning abolished the limp of rats with a lateral-column lesion while reflex-measurement-only controls stayed asymmetrical.
span.quote: The step-cycle asymmetry disappeared in up-conditioned rats and did not change in rats in which the H-reflex was simply measured

span.label: In people with chronic incomplete SCI, 30 down-conditioning sessions reduced the soleus H-reflex in two-thirds of subjects and produced faster, more symmetrical walking with better bilateral EMG modulation, with the reflex still reduced months later.
span.quote: Over 30 conditioning sessions, the soleus H-reflex decreased in two-thirds of the subjects and remained smaller several months later; in these subjects walking speed increased and right-left symmetry improved, with better EMG modulation across the step-cycle in both legs.

span.label: targeted neuroplasticity
span.quote: The essential attribute of these protocols is that they base reward on the activity in a specific CNS pathway (e.g., the soleus H-reflex pathway, a corticospinal pathway).

span.label: negotiated equilibrium hypothesis
span.quote: According to this hypothesis, the brain maintains spinal neurons and synapses in an equilibrium that serves all the behaviors in the current repertoire.

span.label: successful conditioning (operational criterion)
span.quote: Successful conditioning (defined as a change of at least 20% in the correct direction) occurs in 75–80% of the rats (the others remain within 20% of their control value).

span.label: compensatory plasticity
span.quote: These latter changes are likely to represent compensatory plasticity that preserves other behaviors affected by the change in the H-reflex pathway

span.label: task-dependent adaptation and long-term change
span.quote: within-session change (i.e., task-dependent adaptation) that appears after 4–6 conditioning sessions and probably reflects immediate change in cortical influence (e.g., on presynaptic inhibition); and gradual across-session change (i.e., long-term change) that begins after 10–12 sessions and probably reflects spinal cord plasticity

span.label: conditioning mode (up-conditioning vs down-conditioning reward contingency)
span.term: conditioning mode (up-conditioning vs down-conditioning reward contingency)
span.quote: For the next 50 days, it is exposed to the up-conditioning (HRup) or down-conditioning (HRdown) mode, in which a food-pellet reward occurs whenever the H-reflex is above (HRup) or below (HRdown) a criterion value.

span.label: H-reflex size
span.quote: The graphs show average (± SEM) daily H-reflex sizes for 59 successful HRup rats (red upward triangles) and 81 successful HRdown rats (blue downward triangles).

span.label: background EMG level and M-wave size
span.term: background EMG level and M-wave size
span.quote: The background EMG and the M-wave stay constant throughout.

span.label: 75–80% — proportion of subjects in which conditioning succeeded, consistent across all five species/model versions
span.quote: For all versions, conditioning succeeded in 75–80% of the subjects; in the other 20–25%, the reflex remained close to its initial size.

span.label: 175% / 55% — final reflex size as a percentage of baseline in rats and monkeys, for up- and down-conditioning
span.quote: final reflex size was about 175% of its initial value for up-conditioning and 55% for down-conditioning

span.label: 140% / 69% — final reflex size as a percentage of baseline in humans, for up- and down-conditioning
span.quote: In humans, who performed only 3–5% as many trials as the animals, final reflex size averaged 140% for up-conditioning and 69% for downconditioning.

span.label: 10 of 11 — monkeys in which the biceps spinal stretch reflex changed in the rewarded direction in the first demonstration
span.quote: This protocol was successful: in 10 of 11 monkeys, biceps SSR size changed substantially in the correct direction

span.label: 225 — conditioning trials completed per one-hour human session, three sessions per week
span.quote: conditioning occurred in three one-hour sessions per week, each containing 225 conditioning trials

span.label: 2000–6000 — conditioning trials a rat performs per day, yielding 500-1000 rewards
span.quote: A rat averages 2000–6000 trials per day, and the criterion is set to provide 500–1000 rewards per day to satisfy the daily requirement (based on body weight).

span.label: 59 / 81 — number of successfully up-conditioned and down-conditioned rats contributing to the averaged rat curves
span.quote: The graphs show average (± SEM) daily H-reflex sizes for 59 successful HRup rats (red upward triangles) and 81 successful HRdown rats (blue downward triangles).

span.label: 35-year — span of the research programme the review covers, from 1978 basic science to clinical therapy
span.quote: Here we review the 35-year evolution of one promising new approach, operant conditioning of spinal reflexes.
